clue.text: Kids multiplying aboard ship

indicators.note: to be aboard a vessel is to be inside it, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: SS is the standard abbreviation for steamship
tripling is multiplying by three

explanation.surface: Children breeding like rabbits on board a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Multiplying' suggests children breeding, but it means increasing threefold; the steamship abbreviation splits to go round it.
explanation.definitionFit: Striplings are youths or young lads, so the word is a playful synonym for children.

clue.text: Succeeded having edge in church design

indicators.note: something placed in another thing is enclosed by it

blocks.note: S is the usual abbreviation for succeeded in genealogies
CE stands for the Church of England
a hem is the edge of a piece of cloth

explanation.surface: A church plan that worked because of its distinctive edging.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Succeeded' reads as a past-tense verb, but genealogies abbreviate it to a single letter; CE stands for Church of England.
explanation.definitionFit: A scheme is a plan or arrangement, the same sense as a design or plot.

clue.text: Soldiers join forces? Indeed!

blocks.note: the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
to ally is to join forces with someone

explanation.surface: Someone surprised to hear that troops are teaming up.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark and exclamation set up a conversation; the soldiers are the Royal Engineers.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are exclamations of surprise or emphasis that can be used interchangeably in speech.

clue.text: Worker probes corrupt people of influence

indicators.note: corrupt means spoiled or altered from the original form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An employee investigates bent politicians and fixers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corrupt' reads as a verb or adjective about the people; it is the anagram signal for the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Power brokers are those who wield influence behind the scenes, a direct descriptive phrase.

clue.text: Lopped at top, conifer is shorter plant

indicators.note: lopping cuts something off, and at the top means the first letter goes

blocks.note: a fir without its first letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tree that has had its crown cut off ends up shorter.
explanation.walkthrough: FIR loses its F; 'shorter' merely reinforces that the tree is cut down before IS is added.
explanation.definitionFit: The iris is a flowering garden perennial, so plant is a general class containing it.

clue.text: Grumpy creature crossing Severn regularly with fine bird

indicators.note: at regular intervals means every other letter is kept
something crossing a river spans it, so it stretches round the other part

blocks.note: the Grinch is Dr Seuss's bad-tempered creature who stole Christmas
second, fourth and sixth letters
F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine

explanation.surface: A grouch crosses the river Severn with a lovely bird.
explanation.walkthrough: The Severn is Britain's longest river. 'Fine' looks like praise for the bird, but it is the pencil-grade letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The greenfinch is a common European songbird, a member of the finch family.

clue.text: Flawless person conceals primarily rough beginning

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter is wanted
to conceal is to hide something within, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: a gem is a person of great worth
first letter

explanation.surface: A perfect person hides a rough start in life.
explanation.walkthrough: A gem is used of a person who is a treasure.
explanation.definitionFit: A germ is the seed or origin of something, as in the germ of an idea.

clue.text: Stresses of English male with growth stages

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
M is the abbreviation for male
phases are stages of development

explanation.surface: The worries an Englishman suffers as he goes through life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stresses' suggests anxiety, but the definition means emphases placed on words.
explanation.definitionFit: Emphases are points of stress or weight given in speech or writing, the plural noun sense.

clue.text: Scottish son of king simply skinned fish

indicators.note: removing the skin strips the outside, so first and last letters go

blocks.note: Mac in Scottish surnames means son of
K is the chess abbreviation for king
merely without its outer letters

explanation.surface: A Scottish prince prepares fish by just skinning it.
explanation.walkthrough: Simply is MERELY; skinned leaves EREL.
explanation.definitionFit: The mackerel is a common oily sea fish caught in British waters, an example of the category.

clue.text: Chief attendant married enemy, so Spooner said

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so initial sounds trade places

blocks.note: to be married is to have wed
a hater is one who is hostile
swapping W and H sounds

explanation.surface: A senior servant has married their foe, according to Spooner.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening sounds of WED HATER.
explanation.definitionFit: A head waiter is the chief of the waiting staff in a restaurant, the one attending the diners.

clue.text: Mark picked up detailed requirements

indicators.note: to pick up a sound is to hear it, so the word is judged by ear

blocks.note: a speck is a small spot or mark

explanation.surface: A mark noticed on a set of technical requirements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked up' could mean collected, but here it means heard.
explanation.definitionFit: A spec is short for specification, the detailed description of what is required.

clue.text: Struggling since, son paid for action taken suddenly

indicators.note: something struggling is in disarray, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A father in money trouble since his son paid for some reckless act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Struggling' seems to describe someone's finances; it signals rearranging three words.
explanation.definitionFit: A snap decision is a choice made instantly without deliberation, so it is a step taken abruptly.

clue.text: Age-old author imbued NT woman with archaic look

indicators.note: to be imbued with something is to be filled with it, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: Mary is a woman in the New Testament
lo is an old word meaning look or behold

explanation.surface: An old writer gave a New Testament heroine an old-fashioned appearance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look' seems to mean appearance, but it is the archaic exclamation LO.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Thomas Malory wrote Le Morte d'Arthur in the fifteenth century, making him an ancient English writer.

clue.text: This writer and sister go out to find deluge

blocks.note: the setter refers to themself as I
a nun is a religious sister
to date is to go out romantically

explanation.surface: A writer and his sister step outside into a downpour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sister' looks like a sibling; it is a nun, and 'go out' means to court.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean to overwhelm or flood, as with water or a mass of letters.

clue.text: Natural to welcome company for rambling

indicators.note: to welcome a guest is to take them in, so one piece is enclosed

blocks.note: inherent means natural or built in
CO is the abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: It seems natural to invite friends along on a country walk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rambling' suggests hiking, which British people call rambling; here it means disjointed talk.
explanation.definitionFit: Rambling speech wanders without clear logic, so it lacks coherence and is hard to follow.

clue.text: Appearance is reportedly calm making book illustration

indicators.note: reportedly means as it is said, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: a front is an outward show or appearance
taken as written
peace is calm

explanation.surface: An artist's calm look said to suit a book plate.
explanation.walkthrough: Only 'calm' is affected by 'reportedly': PEACE becomes PIECE.
explanation.definitionFit: A frontispiece is the picture facing a book's title page, a specific kind of printed plate.

clue.text: Mischievous shark striking boat with seafood on top

indicators.note: to strike something out is to cross it off, removing letters
in a down answer, what is on top comes first

blocks.note: scampi are breaded langoustines
taken as written
Noah's ark is a boat

explanation.surface: A playful shark attacks a fishing boat with a seafood catch on deck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Striking' looks like an attack, but it means striking out: Noah's vessel is struck from the fish. Scampi are breaded prawns, a British pub staple.
explanation.definitionFit: Scampish means like a scamp, a rascal, so it is a synonym for naughty or playful.

clue.text: Easy chair Charlie occupies on ship

indicators.note: to occupy a space is to sit inside it, so one piece goes within

blocks.note: re means on or about
Charlie is C in the NATO alphabet
a liner is a passenger ship

explanation.surface: Charlie lounges in a deckchair on a cruise.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlie is C in the radio alphabet; 'on' is the Latin-derived RE, as in business letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A recliner is an armchair whose back tilts for lounging, a kind of comfortable seat.

clue.text: Containers of hamster food?

blocks.note: surface: the bowls or packets pet food is sold in
setter's reading: the pockets in a hamster's face where it stores food it gathers

explanation.walkthrough: You think of a pet-shop box, but the hamster carries its own storage in its face.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamsters stuff food into stretchy pockets inside their mouths to carry it home, so these hold their food.

clue.text: What top detective did that’s unpleasant

blocks.note: a top detective runs, that is heads, the department
the CID is the Criminal Investigation Department of British police

explanation.surface: A senior detective did something nasty.
explanation.walkthrough: The chief of detectives ran the CID; 'detective' does double duty.
explanation.definitionFit: Rancid describes stale, rotten food smells, and by extension anything nasty or offensive.

clue.text: Most of London town on good terms

indicators.note: most of something is nearly all of it, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: Welling is a town in the London borough of Bexley

explanation.surface: Most of a London suburb gets on well together.
explanation.walkthrough: Welling is a suburb in south-east London; drop its G.
explanation.definitionFit: Being well in with someone is an informal idiom for being in their favour or friendly.

clue.text: Nonsense a learner put in to spoil explanatory diagram

indicators.note: to put something in is to insert it, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: to mar is to spoil
taken as written
L is for learner, as on L-plates
a key explains the symbols on a map or chart

explanation.surface: A beginner's rubbish spoils a teaching diagram.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put in' looks like a learner's effort; it places the article and the L-plate letter inside the verb for spoil, with the map legend after.
explanation.definitionFit: Malarkey is informal slang for foolish talk or rubbish, a lively synonym.

clue.text: Tiara oddly disappearing in sorcerer’s illusion

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters vanish, so only the even ones remain
placed in another word means enclosed by it

blocks.note: a mage is a sorcerer
second and fourth letters

explanation.surface: A wizard makes a tiara vanish in a conjuring trick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disappearing' sounds like the magic trick itself, but it removes the first, third and fifth letters; the possessive s on sorcerer is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: A mirage is an optical illusion, like water seen in a desert that is not really there.

clue.text: University dons supporting square

indicators.note: to don is to put on clothing, so one piece wraps around the other

blocks.note: for means in favour of
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: College lecturers backing a town square.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dons' looks like academics, but it is the verb to put on: FOR wears U.
explanation.definitionFit: Four is two squared, so it is a square number in the arithmetic sense.

clue.text: Missionary losing track after girl leaves island

indicators.note: losing something means it is taken away, so letters are removed
when someone leaves they are no longer there, so more letters go

blocks.note: taken as written; the island lying inside it is a coincidence of the deletions, not a hidden word
RY is the abbreviation for railway
a miss is a girl or young woman

explanation.surface: A missionary goes astray once a girl has left the island.
explanation.walkthrough: MISSIONARY drops MISS and RY. Apt, since Saint Columba brought Christianity from Iona.
explanation.definitionFit: Iona is a small island in the Inner Hebrides off western Scotland, home of a famous abbey.

clue.text: Show the French murderer turning evil

indicators.note: to turn round is to face the opposite way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a demo is a demonstration or show
la is French for the, feminine
Cain killed his brother Abel in Genesis

explanation.surface: A display in which a French killer goes to the bad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning evil' reads as one phrase; 'turning' belongs to the wordplay and 'evil' stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Demoniacal means devilish or fiendish, like a demon, a strong synonym for wicked.

clue.text: Injury right in back of thigh

indicators.note: something placed in another thing is enclosed by it

blocks.note: the ham is the back of the thigh, as in hamstring
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A hamstring injury sustained just at the back of the leg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back of thigh' looks like where the injury is, but it is the ham.
explanation.definitionFit: Harm is damage or hurt done to a person, a plain synonym for injury.

clue.text: One once flying helicopter an odontologist possesses

indicators.note: to possess is to hold within, so the answer sits inside the phrase

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: An old pilot who once flew a helicopter now owned by a dentist.
explanation.walkthrough: An odontologist is a dentist. 'One once flying' sounds like a retired pilot.
explanation.definitionFit: The pteranodon was a prehistoric flying reptile, now extinct, so it is a creature that used to fly.
